body:
5.1.1 seems a mix of functionality and security.

-  *documentation defines the permitted file types, expected file extensions* " is mostly about functionality and not security. If you support file types that are beyond the list of what is part of documented requirements, as long as those file types are handled properly (per the 5.2.x series), security is not jeopardized at all.
- *expected file extensions, and maximum size (including unpacked size) for each upload feature.* this is more about security, to protect against DOS and I agree it's important. 

Take for example a dropbox that supports every single file type there is. They know how to handle upload safely.

Or take a service that handles many more files types than the product owner wanted. As long as those file types are handled properly - regardless of the documentation - the service is still safe.

comments.body:
And just for reference, here is 5.1.1 today:

| # | Description | Level | #v5.0.be |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: |
| **5.1.1** | Verify that, if the application allows uploading files, the documentation defines the permitted file types, expected file extensions, and maximum size (including unpacked size) for each upload feature. Additionally, ensure that the documentation specifies how files are made safe for end-users to download and process. | 2 | v5.0.be-13.7.3 |

One of the reasons I'm bringing this up is because I have built a large number of file upload systems for large companies without detailed documentation that were not a security risk at all.

I agree for access control and business logic, documentation to map to policy is important. But file upload is more technical in nature and less business logic and I don't see documentation (as described above) as fundamental to security.

> > documentation defines the permitted file types, expected file extensions
> 
> I thought that the intent here was to avoid making it possible to use your application to store/serve malicious files/malwares to users such as,
> 
> * serving malware `.exe`;
> * serving Excel files with malicious macro;
> * serving CSF files with malicious commands/formulas;
> * serving malicious `.apk`;
> * etc.
> 
> if the application only needs to store some type of files (eg. images, videos, music files, etc.).
> 
> Of course there are legitimate use cases for letting a use store all these type of files in an application (and 5.1.1 allows that by documenting that the application must not restrict the range of allowed types).

The point that I am making is - each file type requires specific security requirements to handle properly. And so long as I get that right, I don't need to honor documented list of what files need to be supported to maintain a good security posture. Even if I support more files than the documentation says, as long as I handle those files correctly and do the right validation, we are good to go from a security POV. 

I do not need documentation to describe this - handling uploaded files safely is universally the same for all apps.

Take it as a business logic and input validation requirement. You should accept only the file types that you intend to accept for that precise business process. If you are willing to accept all, no problem with that.

For a reminder: https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/2701#issuecomment-2726365129, #2733

> Take it as a business logic and input validation requirement. You should accept only the file types that you intend to accept for that precise business process. If you are willing to accept all, no problem with that.
> 
> For a reminder: https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/2701#issuecomment-2726365129, #2733

But this has noting to do with security. It's just functionality.
I can support all kinds of files outside of this documentation and still have robust security and little risk.

I don't mind all of these documentation requirements for business logic and access control that can be abused, but supporting extra files types outside of documentation - if validated and handled properly - does not add risk.

My concern is that we are adding a lot of documentation requirements that are just not really necessary for security.

> But this has noting to do with security. It's just functionality.

> I don't mind all of these documentation requirements for business logic and access control that can be abused, but supporting extra files types outside of documentation - if validated and handled properly - does not add risk.

To provide functionality in the expected way (to serve the business need and expectations) is also a security.

> I can support all kinds of files outside of this documentation and still have robust security and little risk.

If you don't have any business process behind that, then your documentation rule must say that you can upload anything from that form.

> My concern is that we are adding a lot of documentation requirements that are just not really necessary for security.

"a lot"? So let's remove all input validation rules, because if you handle them for generating output, you don't need them?

(It was a rhetorical question)

> as long as I handle those files correctly and do the right validation, we are good to go from a security POV.

The point is that since different apps will have widely different requirements for this, the app needs to be clear about it's own expectations as otherwise we are just saying "handle files securely" which is neither testable not implementable.

There is a nearly infinite number of ways to validate strong input. NLP makes this even more complex. 

But there are very specific ways to handle the limited number of file types for file upload. It’s technical not a business logic problem.

For access control I need policy documentation to test, I get that.

But for file upload that is not the case. I know of many testers (for decades) who have effectively tested file upload features without any documentation. Why does ASVS make it required? I don’t get it yet. What are you lacking to get this testing done?

There are even file upload testing toolkits out there to make this easier. It’s part of some DAST tools now as well.

Home come DAST can test for file upload without documentation? It just seems a bit unnecessary for experienced and skilled testers.

And again, there are very few access control testing toolkits because it’s purely business logic. But for file upload security we have (and this list is not exhaustive):1. File Upload Testing in DAST Tools (Mainstream Support)
• MIME-type bypasses
• Extension filtering bypasses
• Content inspection failures
• Remote code execution (e.g., via web shells)
• Storage issues (path traversal, naming collisions, S3 exposure)
• ImageTragick-style attacks (ImageMagick vulnerabilities)
• Virus scan evasion and polyglot file attacks
• Excessive file size or DOS attacks

Examples:
• Burp Suite Pro (via extensions like Upload Scanner or Turbo Intruder)
• OWASP ZAP (can be scripted or enhanced via add-ons)
• Invicti/Acunetix
• AppSpider
• Netsparker
• Burp extensions:
• UploadScanner (by Soroush Dalili) is a standout plugin for fuzzing upload functionality.

2. Specialized File Upload Testing Toolkits

a) UploadScanner (Burp Extension)
• Actively detects:
• Incorrect MIME type enforcement
• Dangerous extensions
• Polyglot files
• Attempts to upload variants and check for access / execution

b) PayloadsAllTheThings – File Upload Cheatsheet
• Huge list of payloads for:
• Filename fuzzing
• Null byte injections
• Bypasses for .htaccess, PHP shell drop, double extensions, etc.

c) Fuxploider
• File upload vulnerability scanner and exploitation tool.
• Supports RCE, shell drop, and extension/MIME bypass testing.

d) Metasploit
• Includes auxiliary modules for file upload exploitation depending on the target tech stack (e.g., PHP, JSP).

Good grief @jmanico, if you think I am opinionated about ASVS, don't get me started on DAST.... 🤣🤣🤣


Maybe take a look at where this requirement came from:
https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/1604

Josh, I listed both DAST tools and pentesting toolkits and resources.

No application was ever insecure ever because of a lack of documentation on file upload security. The security problems show up only when files are validated insecurely.

And my point is, I can list a series of controls to make all file upload features secure, regardless of documentation or files supported. Many sites support file upload of any file type securely, especially in the area of business management software and cloud file management software. GitHub itself does not restrict you from uploading specific file types like images, documents, or executables based solely on the file format.

We did a big push to remove lots of architectural and other non technical requirements, and I am just trying to politely state that some of the documentation requirements are not necessary to reduce risk in modern software.

But I do realize you both disagree. I'm outvoted and I'll close this out.
Do you want to keep this comment and expect a public response?

> Do you want to keep this comment and expect a public response?

I edited the comment to be less controversial.

labels.name: Will be closed if no response/opposite arguments
